title: Yiddish
hookLine: a language built from German, Hebrew and Slavic words, the everyday tongue of Ashkenaz

cards: Chutzpah. Some English speakers use these words without a second thought: carrying something heavy, complaining, a decent human being, a lot of nerve.
Each came into English from a single language, spoken in kitchens, markets and study halls across Ashkenazi Europe.
A grandmother scolding, a peddler bargaining over a coat, a child reciting a lesson, a love letter, a joke that only works in the original. For Ashkenazi Jews it was the sound of home.

teach.b: In Yiddish, the word Yiddish simply means Jewish. It grew among the Jews of Ashkenaz, the German lands, and traveled east with them into Poland and beyond.

Its backbone is German, but it's full of Hebrew and Aramaic words for the things of Jewish life, and it took in Slavic words as Jews settled further east. And it's written in Hebrew letters, right to left.
So a Jew in a Polish town lived with two Jewish languages. One was loshn koydesh, the holy tongue: Hebrew, and the Aramaic of the Talmud, for prayer, Torah and study.

The other was mame loshn, the mother tongue: the language your mother sang to you in, the language of the market, the kitchen and the jokes. Our line today, mama loshen, is an English spelling of that phrase.
Yiddish also opened the texts to people who hadn't been taught Hebrew.
One well-known book, the Tsene-rene, retold the Torah readings in Yiddish, full of stories and commentary, and tradition says women read it on Shabbat and passed it from mother to daughter.
Yiddish was sometimes looked down on, even by Jews, as a mere jargon.

But it's a full language, with its own grammar, songs, newspapers, theater and great writers. And it isn't finished. It's still spoken today, in homes and in schools, and studied by people finding their way back to it.
A mensch, by the way, means more than a person: someone decent, someone you can count on.

how: Yiddish is still the everyday language in some Hasidic homes, and in other Jewish families it lives on in words, songs, sayings and Yiddish classes.

games.q: you are a Jew in a Polish town. it's morning prayers, then the market, then a lullaby at night. which language do you use for what?
o: Hebrew for prayer and study, Yiddish for the market and the lullaby.
Polish for prayer, Hebrew at the market.
games.why: the holy tongue for prayer and Torah, the mother tongue for daily life: two Jewish languages side by side.

practice: Take one Yiddish word, mensch, and say it to yourself quietly. Then bring to mind someone you'd call a mensch, someone who showed up, kept their word, was kind when nobody was watching, and let the word and the face sit together.

wordCard.voice: Yiddish. The everyday language of Ashkenazi Jews, German at its core, full of Hebrew and Slavic words, written in Hebrew letters: the mother tongue beside the holy tongue. Today's word.
